tldr: Instead of manually designing motion sequences, the authors train bimanual policies using only a shared object-centric reward and environment design. Sophisticated coordination—such as handovers and in-hand regrasping—emerges naturally, enabling a single unified policy to succeed across diverse real-world manipulation tasks.
hero_caption: Overall workflow of SimDuoReal. (A) Using a shared object-centric reward, three expert policies (left, right, and handover) are trained in simulation by varying goal-sampling distributions. (B) After transition-state adaptation and distillation via DAgger + RL, a unified policy $\pi_U$ is constructed. (C) On real hardware, the policy directly tracks object trajectories provided by VR or human demonstration videos.
overview:
Bimanual manipulation with multi-fingered hands enables a rich variety of skills, ranging from lifting objects to reorienting them in-hand and transferring them across hands (handovers). However, existing reinforcement learning and imitation learning approaches typically rely on task-specific rewards, finite-state machines, or extensive demonstrations to prescribe exactly which hand grasps an object and when it transfers it. This makes scaling to new tasks extremely difficult.

To address this, the authors focus on an object-centric learning formulation: specifying what should happen to the object rather than how the robot hands must move. Extending previous single-arm approaches to bimanual systems often leads to suboptimal local minima, where a single arm stretches awkwardly to reach far targets without ever learning to hand the object over. SimDuoReal overcomes this challenge through environment design rather than adding complicated reward terms. By simply altering workspace constraints and goal-sampling distributions, single-arm experts and a bimanual handover expert are trained separately under the exact same reward structure. As a result, advanced skills—such as in-hand reorientation to clear grasping space for the receiving hand—emerge spontaneously.

Furthermore, through transition-state fine-tuning to resolve posture mismatches at policy-switching boundaries, all behaviors are distilled into a single unified policy combining DAgger and reinforcement learning. On real hardware, simply tracking target object trajectories provided by VR or human video demonstrations yielded a 76.3% success rate (61 out of 80 trials) across four tasks (barcode scanning, peg insertion, sweeping, and cooking) involving unseen objects, with zero task-specific fine-tuning. This demonstrates that flexible bimanual coordination can be achieved without task-by-task engineering.
contributions: Proposed a framework that learns both single-arm manipulation and bimanual handovers using a shared object-centric reward, driven solely by workspace constraints and goal-sampling distributions without per-behavior reward tuning
Demonstrated that tracking object-pose goals naturally induces emergent behaviors, such as in-hand adjustment to yield grasping space to the receiving hand and pre-grasp manipulation
Constructed a single unified bimanual policy capable of smoothly executing diverse behaviors via transition-state fine-tuning and policy distillation combining DAgger and RL
Achieved a high success rate (76.3%) across four real-world bimanual tasks with unseen objects using only object trajectory commands, requiring no task-specific fine-tuning

sections.heading: Specify what should happen to the object, not how the robot should move
sections.summary: Hand-designing motion sequences or hand-specific rewards for dexterous bimanual manipulation lacks generality. This paper presents an approach where bimanual coordination, including handovers, emerges by pairing an object-centric pose-tracking reward with carefully configured goal distributions in training environments.
sections.details:
For robots to perform daily tasks in homes and factories, flexible coordination—picking up objects, regrasping them, and transferring them across hands—is essential. However, manually engineering motion sequences (such as deciding when the left hand passes an item to the right hand) or tuning task-specific rewards requires enormous engineering effort for every new task.

A promising alternative is an object-centric formulation, where one specifies the desired target state of the object and lets reinforcement learning discover the necessary robot movements. A prior single-arm framework, SimToolReal, showed that tracking random target poses enabled manipulation of unseen tools. However, extending this formulation to bimanual systems across a wide workspace causes exploration to stall: instead of spontaneously discovering handovers to reach distant goals, an arm gets trapped in local minima, straining to reach while making zero progress.

Adding handover-specific reward terms would revert to manual, task-specific engineering. Instead, this work modifies the training environments—specifically goal sampling and workspace constraints—without altering the reward function. By training left- and right-arm experts alongside a handover expert using a shared object-centric objective, the system naturally discovers handover grasps, where the holding hand adjusts the object in-hand to let the other hand grab it easily. Finally, these experts are distilled into a single unified policy that solves four real-world tasks with unseen objects zero-shot, simply prompted by object trajectories from VR or human videos.

sections.heading: At the intersection of bimanual dexterity, object-centric control, and policy distillation
sections.summary: We review three related research areas: bimanual dexterous manipulation, object-centric task specification, and policy distillation. SimDuoReal stands out by training multiple experts with the exact same reward function, acquiring and merging diverse skills solely through differences in environment distributions.
sections.details:
This work builds upon three main research lines:

### Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
Bimanual systems equipped with multi-fingered hands have demonstrated cap unscrewing, tool use, and handovers. However, reinforcement learning methods often rely on task-specific rewards and staged subgoals, while imitation learning requires dedicated human demonstrations for every task. In both cases, humans dictate which hand moves when, making it difficult to expand to new behaviors. In contrast, SimDuoReal uses a single object-centric reward, acquiring skills solely through workspace limits and goal distributions.

### Object-Centric Task Specification
Object-centric formulations have shown success in single-arm in-hand reorientation and tool use (such as SimToolReal). However, they assume a single arm and a single workspace. With two arms, reducing pose error can be achieved either by transporting the object with one hand or transferring it to the other. Without an environment design that enforces handovers, spontaneous handovers do not emerge.

### Expert Policy Integration and Distillation
Training specialized experts and distilling them into a single model, as well as adapting downstream skills to upstream termination states in skill chaining, are common practices in robotics. However, existing methods typically design distinct rewards or reference motions for each skill. In SimDuoReal, the experts differ only in their goal-sampling distributions while sharing the exact same reward function. This allows transition adaptation and RL distillation losses to be optimized consistently under a single unified reward.

sections.heading: Expert training via environment design and seamless policy distillation
sections.summary: Under a shared object-centric reward and representation, three experts are trained by varying the goal-sampling regions. They are then fine-tuned on transition states and distilled into a single policy using DAgger combined with reinforcement learning.
sections.details:
The goal of SimDuoReal is to construct a single bimanual policy capable of tracking desired 6-DoF poses for up to two objects.

### III-A Problem Formulation
The robot observes its joint states, current and target object poses, and geometric features $\mathbf{g}_t$, and outputs relative target commands for the arms and absolute targets $\mathbf{a}_t$ for the hands. A goal is reached when the pose error falls below a threshold $\epsilon$; for handovers, contact with the receiving hand and complete detachment from the releasing hand are additionally required.

### III-B Expert Training via Goal Sampling
The workspace is partitioned into left, right, and shared overlapping regions to train three experts: left arm $\pi_L$, right arm $\pi_R$, and handover $\pi_H$.
- **Single-Arm Experts**: The object starts on the table, and target poses are sampled randomly within that arm's workspace. Pick-up and in-hand reorientation emerge naturally.
- **Handover Expert**: One hand begins holding the object, and goals are sampled deep inside the opposite arm's workspace. Because reaching the goal requires releasing by the handing arm and contact by the receiving arm, the policy naturally learns advanced handover strategies, such as reorienting the object in-hand to avoid obstructing the grasp area.
- **Shared Geometric Representation and Reward**: Feature $\mathbf{g}_t$ includes keypoint distances between each hand and the object surface (target grasp region $S^+$ and non-target region $S^-$), as well as inter-hand keypoint distances. The reward shares a formulation that evaluates progress toward the goal pose, approach to $S^+$, and separation from $S^-$, designed to prevent policies from hovering statically to exploit rewards.

### III-C Expert Integration and Distillation
Sequentially chaining the three experts out of the box causes issues: the handover expert leaves the object in a grasp configuration unfamiliar to the downstream single-arm expert, leading to redundant regrasping or drops.
- **Transition-State Adaptation**: A state pool is collected at expert-switching boundaries, and downstream experts are fine-tuned from these states to adapt to the transition distribution.
- **Distillation via DAgger + RL**: In mixed environments (single-arm scenes, full handover scenes, and concurrent two-arm scenes), a unified policy $\pi_U$ is trained using a combination of DAgger loss (mimicking the experts) and reinforcement learning policy gradient loss. The RL loss enables the policy to recover from its own compounding errors beyond pure imitation.

### III-D Task Generalization via Object-Pose Commands
The trained policy receives target poses at 60 Hz from human VR teleoperation or waypoints extracted from human demonstration videos using pose estimation (FoundationPose). By merely providing target object poses rather than joint trajectories, the policy can execute a wide range of tasks.

Policy inputs include minimum distance vectors $\boldsymbol{\delta}$ from keypoints on the releasing hand $A^-$ and receiving hand $A^+$, as well as inter-hand distances.

sections.heading: Real-world validation across four tasks and simulation ablation studies
sections.summary: In real-world experiments, the unified policy achieved a 76.3% success rate across four bimanual tasks using unseen objects. Simulation benchmarks confirmed that handovers, expert pre-training, transition adaptation, and the RL distillation loss are all essential to performance.
sections.details:
The real-world platform consists of two Franka research arms and two 22-DoF multi-fingered hands (Sharpa Wave), with three RGB-D cameras and an object pose estimation pipeline (FoundationPose, Cutie, Fixed Lag Smoothing) providing tracking at 60 Hz.

### IV-B Real-World Evaluation
A single unified policy—trained only on simple primitive shapes in simulation—was evaluated on four tasks with unseen real objects (20 trials each, 80 trials total):
- **Barcode Scanning**: Grasping a brush and presenting it to a fixed scanner. Handovers are required when starting on the opposite side (80.0% success = 16/20).
- **Peg Insertion**: Holding a block in one hand and a peg in the other, precisely aligning and inserting it (80.0% success = 16/20).
- **Sweeping**: Holding a dustpan in one hand and a broom in the other, coordinating to sweep twice (75.0% success = 15/20).
- **Cooking**: Holding a pan steady with one hand while stirring twice with a spatula in the other (70.0% success = 14/20).
The overall success rate was 76.3% (61/80 trials). Emergent behaviors were observed on real hardware, such as pre-grasp flicking to reorient poorly placed objects and in-hand adjustment before handing over.

### IV-C Simulation Analysis and Ablation
A simulated barcode scanning benchmark (unseen primitive shapes across 3,072 parallel environments) provided detailed analysis:
- **Necessity of Expert Training**: End-to-end RL trained from scratch across the entire domain struggled to gain reward signal and failed completely (episode reward 369 vs. 2,665).
- **Direct Handover vs. Table Regrasping**: A baseline that places the object on the table rather than executing an aerial handover frequently suffered from timeouts and drops, reaching only 60.4% success. Adding direct handover boosted success to 79.4%.
- **Impact of Transition Adaptation**: Fine-tuning on transition states eliminated redundant regrasps, improving success from 79.4% to 84.3% and reducing execution time from 9.1 s to 8.7 s.
- **Distillation Loss Design**: DAgger alone (without RL) achieved 81.6%. Adding the RL loss allowed the student to surpass teacher performance (84.3%), reaching 85.0% success.

sections.heading: Shifting the burden from designing hand coordination to specifying object goals
sections.summary: SimDuoReal shows that grasping, in-hand adjustment, and handovers emerge from an object-centric reward and environment design, enabling a single policy to solve diverse tasks zero-shot. It offers a scalable foundation for controlling dual arms simply by specifying what should happen to the object.
sections.details:
This paper introduced SimDuoReal, a system that acquires sophisticated bimanual coordination without designing behavior-specific rewards. By varying goal-sampling distributions under a single shared object-centric reward, picking up, in-hand reorientation, regrasping, and cooperative handovers emerge naturally.

By distilling these experts into a single policy using transition-state adaptation and DAgger + RL, the system achieved a 76.3% success rate across four real-world tasks with unseen objects and 85.0% in simulation. This suggests a future where roboticists are freed from manually engineering dual-arm coordination sequences, needing only to specify desired object movements.

However, limitations remain: the framework requires accurate 3D object meshes and occlusion-robust multi-camera tracking, cannot easily specify tasks with critical force compliance or fine contact timing using only 6-DoF poses, and relies on external inputs (VR or human videos) to provide target object trajectories.

sections.heading: Appendix: Detailed formulation of the object-centric reward
sections.summary: Detailed mathematical formulation of the reward function shared across all experts. It evaluates pose error, approach to target regions, and detachment from non-target regions, alongside penalties to avoid erratic oscillations and arm collisions.
sections.details:
The appendix details the reward formulation shared across all experts and the student policy.

### Reward Components
- **Pose Progress Reward ($r_t^{\mathrm{pose},j}$)**: Evaluates the maximum displacement among multiple keypoints on the object, awarding positive reward only when improving upon the minimum distance achieved so far in the episode. This prevents policies from hovering statically to collect steady reward.
- **Target Region Contact Reward ($r_t^{\mathrm{con+},j}$)**: Evaluates the approach of the grasping hand (or active single arm) toward the target grasp region $S^+$ on the object.
- **Non-Target Region Detachment Reward ($r_t^{\mathrm{con-},j}$)**: Evaluates the separation distance of releasing elements (such as the handing hand or the table) from the object. A one-time bonus $B_{\mathrm{transfer}}$ is granted upon successful transfer.
- **Regularization and Safety**: A squared joint-velocity penalty $r_t^{\mathrm{vel}}$ is applied, alongside a safety scale factor $r_t^{\mathrm{pen}}$ (approaching 1 as distance increases) that discounts the overall reward whenever the closest distance between the two arms or hands enters a danger zone, preventing self-collisions.

takeaways: Advanced bimanual coordination—such as reorienting an object in-hand to hand it over cleanly—emerges naturally from workspace limits and goal sampling without hand-designed motion rules
Learning full-body bimanual manipulation end-to-end from scratch is brittle; training specialized experts under a shared reward and distilling them provides a robust learning strategy
When chaining modular experts, transition-state adaptation fine-tuning closes distribution shifts at switching boundaries, substantially raising success rates and cutting redundant motions
An object-centric 6-DoF pose-tracking interface enables zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks and objects simply by commanding trajectories from VR or human videos
limitations: Requires accurate 3D object meshes and a multi-camera pipeline for robust 60 Hz real-time 6-DoF pose tracking under hand occlusions
Task specification is limited to geometric 6-DoF trajectories, making it difficult to directly handle tasks requiring precise force compliance or fine-grained contact timing
Target object trajectories must be supplied externally via VR teleoperation or human demonstration videos, lacking autonomous trajectory planning
